consts.name: dmkRegionalMaterialCount
consts.comment: the regional material count - seven lower-class materials: pounded tree bark, flax, wool, woven horse-hair, furs, paper, and hemp (print capture p. 306)

consts.name: dmkCommonColorCount
consts.comment: the common color count - five common dye colors: browns, ochres, yellows, grays, and blues (print capture p. 306)

consts.name: dmkNamedReligionCount
consts.comment: the named religion count - five named: The Way, The Path of Enlightenment, The Eight Million Gods, ancestor worship, and the cult of the state (print capture p. 310)

consts.name: dmkCommonerPunishmentCount
consts.comment: the commoner punishment count - nine: execution, branding, loss of the hands, fines, imprisonment, banishment, slavery, the heavy yoke, and public announcements (print capture p. 311)

consts.name: dmkHigherClassPunishmentCount
consts.comment: the higher-class punishment count - four: house arrest, banishment, loss of position, and honorable death (print capture p. 311)

bools.name: dmkClothingStatusDoctrine
bools.comment: the clothing status doctrine - clothing as practicality plus the identification of rank, the decoration quality and materials indicating the wearer's status (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkCommonMaterials
bools.comment: the common clothing materials - cotton and silk the most common (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkRegionalMaterials
bools.comment: the regional lower-class materials - pounded tree bark, flax, wool, woven horse-hair, furs, paper, and hemp, confined to specific regions and the lower classes (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkLeatherDoctrine
bools.comment: the leather doctrine - heavy leathers for durability, soft deerskin for flexibility or lavish decoration (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkWhiteMourning
bools.comment: the white mourning rule - white the color of mourning, so nearly all cloth is dyed, the dyes from flowers, nuts, barks, woods, and minerals (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkCommonColors
bools.comment: the common colors - browns, ochres, yellows, grays, and blues common, the brighter greens, pinks, and reds rarer and worn by the higher station (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkTrouserDoctrine
bools.comment: the trouser doctrine - the short wrap-around cotton trousers tied with strings, loose for wading the paddies, striped or patterned, the peasant wear of both sexes (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkRobeDoctrine
bools.comment: the robe doctrine - the commoners' short belted robe; the wealthier omitting trousers for long robes; the nobility's layered robes of different colors peeking at sleeves and collar, an art of the ladies' court; the wide open sleeves as cold-weather muffs since gloves are not worn and as pockets for handkerchief and cash (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkMinoRaincloak
bools.comment: the mino raincloak - the peasants' rain cloak of layered straw (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkFootwearDoctrine
bools.comment: the footwear doctrine - the woven straw sandal simplest and most common; the straw or wooden-block sandals of Kozakura; the soft-leather or cloth slippers of the refined and the soldiers' short boots of Shou Lung and T'u Lung; the fur-wrapped leather boots of the cold north (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkHatDoctrine
bools.comment: the hat doctrine - hats a clear sign of status; the peasants' round broad-rimmed straw or bamboo hats doubling as baskets; the shukenja and monks' basket hats; the nobles' small styled hats; the gentlemen's huge-rimmed horsehair hats; the scarf or cloth for rain (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkMaleBeauty
bools.comment: the male beauty doctrine - grace and beauty the pride of men of rank, the pale complexion best, the plucked eyebrows, the perfume-mixing skill, most falling short of the ideal (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkFemaleBeauty
bools.comment: the female beauty doctrine - the blackened teeth as standard with the pearly white smile an unfortunate flaw of the west, the plucked and repainted thin-line eyebrows, the powdered palest faces (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkHairDoctrine
bools.comment: the hair doctrine - the topknot of rank held with carved pins, the Kozakura topknot-cutting punishment for minor offenses shaming the man before his lord; the children's single lock, crown for boys and ear for girls; the samurai's coming-of-age forehead shave; the peasants' queue; the women's long flowing hair as beauty and station, cut short in mourning or upon the nun's veil; the priests' shaven heads (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkNoChurchConcept
bools.comment: the no-church concept - the average man not attending, the church as a separate entity strange to him, religion organized on such a scale nonexistent, yet piety and respect intact (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkManyReligionsPractice
bools.comment: the many-religions practice - few commoners follow strictly one religion, taking no chances, making offerings, hearing sermons, celebrating holy days, and praying at the temples of many different religions without it being unusual (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkReligiousTolerance
bools.comment: the tolerance doctrine - the religions extremely tolerant of one another, temples side by side, sects adopting other practices and re-explaining them, minor gods adopted as forms of deities already worshiped, the clergy alone faithful to one (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkSectDoctrine
bools.comment: the sect doctrine - the sects sharing goals but disputing methods, the chanting phrases, the different phrase, the breathing and physical exercises, the fierce rivalries, feuds, and violent clashes, sects of the same religion often more hostile to each other than to entirely different religions (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkCourtStructure
bools.comment: the court structure - the law court of every province and major city headed by the magistrate with broad powers, the scholar by examinations, the noble appointee, the daimyo, the sage, or the village headman, with bailiff, constables, outcast assistants, and secretaries (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkEvidenceGathering
bools.comment: the evidence gathering - the bailiff and constables gathering evidence and holding it, arresting or ordering witnesses, no protection from arrest save the displeasure of the magistrate, and the trial date set with little delay (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkNoLawyers
bools.comment: the no-lawyers trial - the accused and accuser stating their cases, the magistrate asking all questions, the ordered beatings and torture to aid memory and for the out-of-order, the witnesses questioned with force to extract testimony, the bailiff keeping order and administering the beatings (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkSpeakWithDeadTestimony
bools.comment: the speak-with-dead testimony - the murder-case spellcaster summoned, the dead's testimony accepted as fact, spells determining the truth of statements, the secretaries stating the laws and previous cases (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkClassDoubleStandard
bools.comment: the class double standard - the higher rank receiving special considerations, the commoner's crimes not crimes for the warrior class, the Kozakuran samurai's right to cut down an insulting or truculent commoner without a murder charge, the vendetta with approvals, yet gambling and drunkenness more severe for the samurai who has broken his trust (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkPunishmentDoctrine
bools.comment: the punishment doctrine - punishments fixed by law with the magistrate's power to alter severity, the commoner punishments of execution, branding, loss of the hands, fines, imprisonment, banishment, slavery, the heavy yoke, and the public announcements, the higher classes' house arrest, banishment, loss of position, and honorable death, the treasonous samurai forced to public humiliation in execution (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkCivilMediation
bools.comment: the civil mediation - the magistrate hearing civil and criminal cases, the harsh court treatment driving settlements through the priest or village-headman mediator, binding only if both parties agree, else the court (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkCollectiveResponsibility
bools.comment: the collective responsibility - the entire family, village, or group punished for the criminal's actions, the banished samurai's family banished with him, the murderer's village punished, the commoners loathe to aid criminals, the policy effective (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkVendettaDoctrine
bools.comment: the vendetta doctrine - the vendetta officially sanctioned in some lands such as Kozakura, a required part of the samurai's honor to avenge the murdered or slain relation (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkVendettaRankRule
bools.comment: the vendetta rank rule - the avenger cannot be of higher rank than the person slain, the eldest son unable to avenge a younger brother, the direct retainer unable to avenge a lesser retainer (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkVendettaApproval
bools.comment: the vendetta approvals - release from the lord's service by application, granted if the cause is just and the services not required, the reentry with no penalties and perhaps renown, the local government's approval normally given with little question but deniable if the hunted is valuable or a friend, the unapproved avenger arrested for murder (print capture pp. 306-312)

bools.name: dmkVendettaDuel
bools.comment: the vendetta duel - with all approvals the challenge to a duel to the death at any time, everything legally done so the winner is not charged with murder, and any number of seconds assisting so it need not be one-on-one (print capture pp. 306-312)

examples.note: the punishment ladder - the commoner punishments minus the higher-class punishments is five
the common colors equal the named religions - both five
the regional materials plus the named religions is twelve
